q: For accounting the salary payable in March to staff in the same month (which actually paid in April of next year), which suspense head is operated?

Related exam fact: Demands Payable always carries a credit balance on the expenditure side, representing undischarged liabilities at month end.

q: Government accounts are maintained on ___basis while Railway accounts are maintained on ____basis
e: The correct answer is Cash; Accrual. The correct option is (A): Government accounts are maintained on cash basis while Railway accounts are maintained on accrual basis. Railways recognise earnings when raised and expenditure when the liability arises (e.g., March salary booked in March through Demands Payable), whereas government accounts record only cash flows. Related exam fact: this is exactly why link suspense heads like Traffic Account, Labour and Demands Payable exist — to bridge accrual railway books with cash government books.

q: The suspense head Traffic Accounts always has balance and represents ____earnings
e: The correct option is (C): the Traffic Account suspense head always has a debit balance and represents unrealised earnings. Station earnings are debited to Traffic Account when raised; the debit persists until the cash is actually realised and cleared. A suspense head temporarily parks transactions whose final head is not yet known; the balance must be cleared by adjustment, not left indefinitely.

q: Labour and Demands Payable suspense heads have a ___balance on expenditure side and represent liability at the end of the month
e: Option B (Credit; undischarged) is the correct choice. The correct option is (B): Labour and Demands Payable suspense heads carry a credit balance on the expenditure side, representing undischarged liability at the end of the month. Wages earned and amounts payable but not yet paid are liabilities, hence credit balances. When paid, the heads are debited and cleared. Related exam fact: March salary payable in April is the textbook example — booked to Demands Payable in March itself on accrual basis.

q: Miscellaneous advances (Rev) will have -----balance; while Deposit Miscellaneous will have -----balance
e: Debit; Credit — that is the right answer. The correct option is (C): Miscellaneous Advances (Revenue) has a debit balance, while Deposit Miscellaneous has a credit balance. Advances represent money paid out and awaiting recovery or adjustment (debit = asset-like), whereas deposits represent money received from outsiders held as liability (credit). Mixing the two upsets the trial balance logic. Related exam fact: debits to Deposit Miscellaneous represent refunds of earlier credits or write-offs — the mirror image of an advance's behaviour.

q: Debits to Deposit Miscellaneous will represent
e: The correct option is (C) Both of these. Refunds repay fares/freight collected in excess or for services not rendered, after verifying the claim against records. e: The correct option is (B) Deposit Miscellaneous (PF). q: All capital transactions, except suspense heads, are closed to
e: The correct answer is Capital Outlay. The correct option is (B) Capital Outlay. Related exam fact: the three-way closing rule is — capital (non-suspense) to Capital Outlay, revenue (non-suspense) to Net Revenue, and suspense heads to Balance (except Transfer Railways). q: All revenue transactions, except suspense heads are closed to
e: Net Revenue — that is the right answer. The correct option is (A) Net Revenue. Suspense items remain under 'Balance' until adjusted. Related exam fact: Net Revenue is the starting point for working out the surplus or deficit and for appropriations to reserve funds like DRF, DF and the Pension Fund. They stay open until cleared. Related exam fact: Transfer Railways is the exception because inter-railway settlements close to the Miscellaneous Government Account on zonal railways. q: Transactions under 'Deposits with Reserve Bank (Rlys)' is closed to
e: The correct answer is Miscellaneous Government Account. The correct option is (B) Miscellaneous Government Account. q: Credits to DRF are

options.C: Interest accrued on fund balances and loans

e: A&C — that is the right answer. The correct option is (D) A and C. Credits to the Depreciation Reserve Fund are the annual appropriation from revenue (the depreciation charge on assets) plus interest accrued on the fund's balances and on loans out of the fund. Renewals and replacements are debited to DRF, so these credits are what keep the fund replenished. Related exam fact: DRF exists precisely so that asset renewals do not burden current working expenses — the cost is spread over the asset's life through yearly appropriations.

q: Credits to DF are

options.B: Interest accrued on fund balances and loans

e: Option C (A&B) is the correct choice. The correct option is (C) A and B. Credits to the Development Fund are the appropriation from revenue surplus and interest accrued on the fund's balances and loans. DF finances passenger/staff amenities, unremunerative projects and safety works — expenditure that is socially desirable rather than remunerative. Related exam fact: unlike DRF (renewals) and the Pension Fund (retirement benefits), DF is the fund for developmental and welfare-type capital works.

q: Credits to Pension fund are
e: Credits to the Pension Fund comprise the appropriation from Revenue/Capital, interest accrued on the fund balances, and amounts transferred from the contributory Provident Fund — hence all of these.
